blocks.text: 1. This high-pitched, harsh airway sound usually signals partial blockage of the upper airway. It may be described as sharp or squeaky, and is often more pronounced when the child is crying or lying down. (Listen to an example HERE.) (Note to devs: Please link to “Lung Sounds Quiz AUDIO 1” mp3)

Stridor occurs due to inflammation or obstruction of the upper airway and produces a sharp, musical sound. While it can be biphasic, it’s usually most noticeable on inspiration. Stridor has multiple causes including (but not limited to!) viral inflammation (like croup), foreign body aspiration, allergic swelling of the airway, or even congenital airway abnormalities (like laryngomalacia).
2. Which of the following is NOT true regarding wheezing?
It is commonly heard in children with asthma and bronchiolitis
It is more pronounced on inspiration when airways are naturally more narrowed
It is a continuous, high-pitched whistling sound
Diffuse wheezing often indicates causes like asthma, allergic reaction, or viral infection while localized wheezing may indicate foreign body aspiration
Wheezing is a sound created by turbulent air movement through narrowed lower airways. It is more pronounced on expiration, not inspiration, since that is when airways are naturally more narrowed.

3. Sometimes described as sounding like Velcro, intermittent pops, or like rubbing your hair between your fingers next to your ear, this discontinuous lung sound is often indicative of fluid accumulated in the alveoli and small airways. (Listen to an example HERE.) (Note to devs: Please link to “Lung Sounds Quiz AUDIO 2” mp3)

Crackles are the result of collapsed alveoli or small airways “popping” open, primarily heard during inspiration. They are often further categorized as “fine” or “course” depending on the pitch and duration of the pops.
4. Which of the following describes rhonchi most accurately?
Discontinuous, low-pitched sounds resulting from intermittent bronchospasm
Almost exclusively heard on inspiration, these low “wet” sounds are the result of increased mucus burden in children with difficulty clearing secretions
Deep rumbling or snoring-like sounds coming from the larger airways that often improve after suctioning
Dry, harsh, grating sounds that are typically localized to a specific area of the chest and heard during both inspiration and expiration.

Rhonchi result from air moving through large airways that are partially blocked by mucus/secretions. So they are the result of congestion rather than bronchospasm. While rhonchi are often the result of excess mucus, they are not exclusively heard on inspiration. While they can be heard on both inspiration and expiration, they are often more prevalent on expiration. Since they are due to secretions, they are “wet” sounds and are not like pleural rub (which can be described as dry, harsh, and grating).

blocks.text: 1. Which ventilator settings affect oxygenation? Select all that apply.

Explanation: Any setting that changes mean airway pressure (MAP) can affect oxygenation. In the video, we used a pressure‑versus‑time curve to visualize the Area Under the Curve (AUC), but a volume‑versus‑time curve would work as well—the key concept is area under the curve (AUC).  Pressure Support (PS) is another way of taking a breath; it often generates slightly lower pressures than a mandatory breath, but it still contributes to MAP, and therefore oxygenation.
2. Which TWO ventilator settings have the biggest impact on oxygenation? (select two)

Explanation: FiO₂ directly increases the amount of oxygen delivered to the alveoli, while PEEP most greatly impacts the mean airway pressure (biggest component of the area under the curve!) and helps keep alveoli open, improving gas exchange. Together, these two settings have the largest and most immediate effect on oxygenation.
3. What is the main cause of hypoxia in an infant with bronchiolitis?
Ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) mismatch – primarily a V problem
Ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) mismatch – primarily a Q problem

Explanation: In bronchiolitis, mucous plugging and airway inflammation impair ventilation to parts of the lung, while perfusion remains relatively preserved. This mismatch between ventilation and perfusion leads to hypoxia.
4. What is the main cause of hypoxia in a 9-month old, ex-25 week  infant with chronic lung disease who is experiencing a severe pulmonary hypertensive crisis?
Ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) mismatch – primarily a V problem
Ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) mismatch – primarily a Q problem

Explanation: In pulmonary hypertension, blood flow is redirected away from well‑ventilated alveoli due to high pulmonary vascular resistance. This creates a perfusion problem, leading to V/Q mismatch and hypoxia.

5. What is the MOST LIKELY cause of hypoxia in an obese adolescent male post‑tonsillectomy/adenoidectomy (TNA) for severe OSA, who is saturating 85% on room air? You can hear him snoring down the hall…
Ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) mismatch – primarily a V problem
Ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) mismatch – primarily a Q problem

Explanation: Upper airway obstruction from residual anesthesia or severe OSA (possibly, in part, due to body habitus) leads to inadequate ventilation and CO₂ retention, resulting in hypoxia. It is also important to consider post‑obstructive pulmonary edema (a topic for another day), which would cause diffusion limitation due to fluid in the alveoli making oxygen transfer more difficult. While post-obstructive pulmonary edema is the main reason these patients are monitored in the PICU and should not be missed, this is less likely than hypoventilation. This should come to mind when repositioning and fixing the hypoventilation does not work! Time for that CXR.
A chest X‑ray of an intubated pediatric patient with bronchiolitis is shown below.
The child has copious secretions and is saturating 82%, requiring frequent FiO₂ increases. Which ventilator setting change would be MOST effective for improving this child’s oxygen saturation?

Explanation: Atelectasis causes hypoxia due to ventilation/perfusion mismatch from under‑ventilated lung regions (a primary V problem). Increasing PEEP helps recruit collapsed alveoli, reducing V/Q mismatch and improving oxygenation more effectively than simply increasing FiO₂.

blocks.text: Hypercarbia (elevated PCO2) most commonly indicates problems with ____
Explanation: Refer back to the oxygenation and ventilation videos in Lake Mucosa for questions.
Ventilation is best denoted by which of the following?

Explanation: Whenever you have a hypercarbic patient, it’s important to think back to the ventilation video/reading for the minute ventilation equation. Is there something that is inhibiting the patient from breathing a sufficient number of times or minute (e.g., did you paralyze the patient and forget to increase the RR?) or from delivering appropriate tidal volumes to the lungs (e.g., are secretions blocking appropriate aeration of the lungs? Is compliance poor and you need to increase PIP or Vt to support the patient?). One of the reasons PRVC is a go-to mode of ventilation in PICU is that it guarantees minute ventilation. While PC modes do deliver tidal volumes, PIP alone does not guarantee minute ventilation.
When a ventilator is alarming for minute ventilation, which patient or ventilator parameter is most likely to indicate the problem?
Difference between inhaled tidal volume (VTi) and exhaled tidal volume (VTe)

Explanation: If the minute ventilation alarm is going off, the MV equation suggests either the RR or the Vt set is not being delivered to the patient. Most commonly, this means the tidal volume is not reaching the patient. The first act should be ensuring that this is a vent problem (condensation in the tubing, etc) and not a patient problem (the ETT or trach is no longer in the correct position, secretions needing suctioning). This can be most easily done by inspecting the tube position and the end tidal CO2. Remember that TCOMs do not rise in real time like an EtCO2 does and should not be used to determine if your artificial airway is functioning!
When a patient needs additional support with ventilation, which answer choice will NOT typically assist them in blowing off CO2?
Decreasing the iTime, allowing more time for exhalation (“more eTime”)
Increasing the PEEP to increase mean airway pressure
Suctioning the airway. Removing secretions blocking the upper airway may assist delivering the set tidal volumes to the lungs
Increasing the PIP in a PC mode of ventilation to allow for larger tidal volumes in a lung with good compliance

Explanation: Whenever thinking about ventilation, recall the MV formula from the ventilation video. Answer choices (a), (d), and (e) all reference Vt and RR. Answer choice (b) indirectly affects exhaled Vt by allowing the patient more time to exhale, effectively letting them blow off more CO2, therefore improving ventilation. Answer choice (c) is a maneuver to increase oxygenation more than ventilation.

blocks.text: Format: drag each item into one of three buckets: Strong Evidence/ Limited Evidence / Not recommended
Items 1–21 with correct bucket and short rationale
Perform hand hygiene before and after touching the patient’s airway.
Rationale: Hand hygiene is the single most effective measure to prevent healthcare-associated infections and must be done before/after airway care.
Elevate the head of bed to 30 degrees unless contraindicated.
Rationale: Semi-recumbent positioning reduces aspiration risk and VAP incidence when tolerated.
Change ventilator circuits routinely every 48 hours.
Rationale: Routine circuit changes increase manipulation and contamination risk; change only if soiled or malfunctioning.
Assess daily readiness to extubate and attempt spontaneous breathing trials when appropriate.
Rationale: Reducing duration of mechanical ventilation lowers VAP risk; daily assessment expedites weaning.
Perform oral care with saline/moistened swabs every 4–8 hours for intubated children.
Rationale: Routine oral hygiene removes secretions and reduces bacterial colonization; frequency adjusted per patient.
Monitor cuff pressures regularly for cuffed endotracheal tubes (maintain within recommended range).
Rationale: Proper cuff pressure prevents micro-aspiration while avoiding mucosal injury; check routinely.
Use prophylactic systemic antibiotics to prevent VAP in ventilated patients.
Rationale: Routine prophylactic antibiotics increase resistance and are not shown to prevent VAP.
Minimize sedation and perform daily sedation interruption when clinically appropriate.
Rationale: Sedation minimization reduces ventilator days and associated VAP risk.
Use closed suction systems for all patients to prevent VAP.
Rationale: Closed systems can reduce environmental contamination and are useful for unstable patients, but benefit for VAP prevention is mixed; choose per policy and patient needs.
Obtain endotracheal/tracheal aspirate culture before starting antibiotics for suspected VAP, if safe.
Rationale: Cultures guide therapy and stewardship but may not always be feasible in unstable patients — clinical judgment required.
Routinely change heat–moisture exchanger (HME) filters daily.
Rationale: Routine daily changes are unnecessary and may increase manipulation; follow manufacturer/unit protocols.
Routinely disconnect the ventilator circuit to reposition the patient.
Rationale: Unnecessary disconnections increase contamination and loss of PEEP; avoid and plan care to minimize breaks.
Use enteral feeding protocols and prefer gastric feeding over parenteral nutrition when feasible.
Rationale: Enteral feeding preserves gut integrity and immunity; aspiration risk requires protocols and monitoring, so it’s context-dependent.
Apply contact precautions for patients colonized or infected with multidrug-resistant organisms.
Rationale: Contact precautions limit spread of MDR organisms in the unit and protect vulnerable ventilated patients.
Use prophylactic inhaled antibiotics in intubated patients to prevent VAP.
Rationale: Routine prophylactic inhaled antibiotics are not recommended due to lack of definitive benefit and risk of resistance.
Perform oral suctioning of pooled secretions prior to repositioning or suctioning ETT.
Rationale: Removing pooled secretions reduces aspiration risk during movement or airway manipulation.
Use a routine schedule of ventilator circuit humidifier changes (e.g., every 24 hours) regardless of condition.
Rationale: Routine frequent changes are unnecessary; change when contaminated, malfunctioning, or per manufacturer guidance.
Use spontaneous awakening and breathing trial coordination (paired SBT/SAT) as part of daily practice when feasible.
Rationale: Coordinated SBT/SAT reduces ventilation duration but must be individualized in PICU patients with variable conditions.
Provide staff education and bundle checklists with regular audit and feedback on VAP prevention practices.
Rationale: Education and compliance monitoring are proven to improve adherence to prevention bundles and reduce VAP rates.
Use prone positioning routinely to prevent VAP.
Rationale: Prone positioning is a therapeutic maneuver for severe ARDS, not a VAP prevention strategy, and has specific indications/risks.
Start empiric broadspectrum antibiotics immediately for any new ventilator-associated change without obtaining cultures.
Rationale: Empiric therapy may be necessary in unstable patients, but ideally obtain cultures first to target therapy and support stewardship.

paragraphs: Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia is defined as a new pneumonia occurring in a patient who has been mechanically ventilated for more than 48 hours.
It is one of the most common hospital-acquired infections in the pediatric population and poses a substantial risk for patients in the PICU.
VAP is particularly concerning due to its association with increased mortality, prolonged hospital stays, and elevated healthcare costs.
It is the second most frequent hospital-acquired infection (HAI) in the Pediatric Intensive Care Unit (PICU) .
slides.text:
Definition
Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia is defined as a new pneumonia occurring in a patient who has been mechanically ventilated for more than 48 hours.
It is one of the most common hospital-acquired infections in the pediatric population and poses a substantial risk for patients in the PICU.
VAP is particularly concerning due to its association with increased mortality, prolonged hospital stays, and elevated healthcare costs.
It is the second most frequent hospital-acquired infection (HAI) in the Pediatric Intensive Care Unit (PICU) .

paragraphs: VAP occurs in approximately 5-14% of pediatric patients who are mechanically ventilated for over 48 hours . It affects up to 1 in 10 patients on invasive mechanical ventilation.
The incidence of VAP can be higher in children compared to adults, given their unique physiology and potential comorbidities.

The pathogens responsible for VAP can vary, but often include bacteria like Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Staphylococcus aureus, and various enteric gram-negative bacteria. Understanding these pathogens is crucial for appropriate treatment and prevention.

paragraphs: Now, let’s discuss the potential sequelae of VAP. Patients can experience:
Prolonged Ventilation: Increased duration of mechanical ventilation contributes to further complications.
Increased Length of Stay: VAP can lead to a longer hospital stay, which strains healthcare resources.
Higher Mortality Rates: In severe cases, VAP can be fatal, especially in immunocompromised patients or those with underlying conditions.
Long-term Pulmonary Issues: Some studies suggest that survivors may experience residual pulmonary dysfunction, impacting long-term quality of life.
Increased Health Care Costs: Managing VAP can result in significant financial burdens on families and healthcare systems.
Understanding these sequelae underscores the importance of prevention and early detection. As PICU nurses, you play a vital role in implementing preventive measures and monitoring at-risk patients

Long-term Pulmonary Issues: Some studies suggest that survivors may experience residual pulmonary dysfunction, impacting long-term quality of life.
Increased Health Care Costs: Managing VAP can result in significant financial burdens on families and healthcare systems.

Understanding these sequelae underscores the importance of prevention and early detection. As PICU nurses, you play a vital role in implementing preventive measures and monitoring at-risk patients

Scenario 1: High Peak Pressure Alarm (Child with Asthma)
Patient is a 6-year-old asthmatic in the PICU, room #555, named Carl Sagan. He is intubated and mechanically ventilated.
Ventilator Alarm: High Peak Pressure, Paw High
Pt experiencing increased work of breathing
Pt becoming agitated despite sedation gtts
Bronchospasm causing increased airway resistance. This explains all assessment findings as well as the alarm itself. It also is in line with the patient’s known respiratory condition.
Urgency: Urgent – not immediately life-threatening, but requires prompt response to prevent escalation.

“Hi, this is the RN taking care of Carl Sagan in 555. He is our 6-year-old intubated status asthmaticus who was admitted from the ED this morning. His ventilator is alarming for high peak pressures and his sats have dropped to the high 80’s.”

“Carl was intubated in the ED earlier today for worsening respiratory distress. He’s currently on pressure-controlled ventilation and has been receiving continuous albuterol. Up until now, he’s been pretty calm and vitals have looked good.”

“On auscultation, I hear diffuse expiratory wheezing. He’s having moderate to severe retractions that started subcostal and are moving up. His sats, which were in the high 90s have dropped to the high 80s and are falling. On the vent, peak pressures have increased significantly, tidal volumes are decreasing, and the patient is becoming more agitated.”
“I’d like RT/First Call to come to bedside and assess Carl for possible worsening bronchospasm. I think he needs additional respiratory treatments and possibly ventilator adjustments.”
Scenario 2: Low Minute Volume Alarm (Premature Neonate)

Patient is a four-day-old 28-weeker in the NICU, room #678, named BG-Carol Ride (baby’s name is “Sally”). She was intubated for respiratory distress shortly after birth and was stabilized in the South side of the NICU. After routine repositioning, the ventilator starts alarming.
Ventilator Alarm: Low (Expiratory) Minute Volume, low MVe
Infant bradycardic (HR was 140s, now 90s and falling)
Leak around ETT (assess cuff pressure if applicable)

Unplanned extubation (tube dislodgement). This explains all assessment findings and is in line with recent patient care (repositioning). Nurse should quickly assess ventilator expiratory tubing integrity, but UE is most likely.
Urgency: Emergent – life-threatening, requires immediate response

“This is the nurse for 678, Baby Girl Carol Ride. Her ventilator is alarming for low minute volumes. She’s bradying and desatting and if you want to start heading this way, that would be great. I am about to hit Staff Assist because I think she’s self-extubated.”
“Sally was intubated for respiratory distress and was previously stable on current ventilator settings.”

“She’s not apneic, she’s actually working pretty hard, but I’m seeing poor chest rise and on auscultation she isn’t moving much air. I attempted to suction and could pass the catheter but got nothing. The ETT marking looks to be 2 cm less than on my previous assessment and she is becoming increasingly unstable. Sally’s HR is in the 90s, sats in the low 70s, and both continue to drift down.”

“I am putting a PediCap on as we speak and will try to bag through the tube. I’d like to pull the tube if I don’t get color change and begin BVM ventilation. I need RT and First Call at bedside immediately along with the airway cart.”
Scenario 3: High Respiratory Rate Alarm (Child with Sepsis/Pneumonia)
The patient is a 10-year-old named John Glenn with septic shock and pneumonia currently in the PICU in room #546. He is intubated and mechanically ventilated.
Overly sensitive interpretation of breaths (ex: wet flow meter)

Unclear, too many causes to rule out all but one. However, given the assessment findings, this is likely generalized deterioration of clinical condition (fever, pain, hypercapnia, increased O2 needs = inadequate vent support) and not a ventilator sensor/meter error.
Urgency: Semi-Urgent – not immediately life-threatening, but requires prompt response.
“Hi, this is the RN taking care of John Glenn. He’s our 10-year-old sepsis pneumonia in 546. The vent is alarming for high respiratory rate, and John is increasingly tachypneic and agitated.”

“John was transferred from the floor yesterday for worsening respiratory status related to pneumonia and septic shock. He was intubated later that afternoon and he had been stable most of the morning.”

“He’s been slowly worsening over the course of the afternoon and now he’s breathing in the upper 50s over the ventilator, oxygen needs have increased and I’ve titrated the FiO2 from 40% to 60% to maintain sats in the 90s, his end-tidal is rising, and he appears uncomfortable despite his sedative drips. He has also become febrile again with a temp just now of 38.5°C”
“I’d like RT to come to bedside and assess so we can present possible ventilator adjustments and sedation management changes to the First Call.”

Patient is a 2-week-old term neonate in room #512 the CVICU named BB-Blanche Lovell (baby’s name is “Jim”). He is intubated and mechanically ventilated.
Stable pre and post-ductal oxygen saturations
Appropriate chest rise, manual count of RR (60) does not match ventilator (vent is reading RR >100)
Breath sounds unchanged from previous assessment (clear bilaterally)
Inaccurate overly sensitive interpretation of breaths (ex: wet flow sensor)
Due to patient’s stable condition and the RR mismatch between the vent and the eyes-on assessment, it is likely that condensation in the flow sensor is causing an inaccurate reading.
Urgency: Non-urgent - requires response as soon as time allows
“Hi, this is the nurse taking care of Baby Boy Blanche Lovell in 512. I’m calling because he’s having persistent high respiratory rate alarms on the ventilator. It’s reading rates over 100.”
“Jim is two weeks old, ventilated, and has been stable on my shift.”

“He remains clinically stable with normal chest rise, clear breath sounds bilaterally, stable sats both pre and post-ductally, appropriate for his defect. I manually counted his respirations at 60 so the alarms do not appear consistent with the patient’s actual respiratory effort. I think the flow sensor may need to be recalibrated.”
“I’d like RT to come to bedside when it’s convenient to recalibrate this flow sensor please.”
Scenario 5: High Pressure Alarm (Toddler with Pneumonia)

Patient is a 3-year-old with pneumonia named Katherine Johnson. She is trach/vent dependent at home and was admitted to room #570 in the PICU two days ago following a clinic visit. She remains trached and mechanically ventilated.
Ventilator Alarm: High Peak Pressure, Paw High
Decreased oxygen saturation to 82% and falling
Minimal secretions visible in ET tube initially

Due to the assessment findings, particularly the sudden clinical change in combination with the inability to easily pass the suction catheter, there is likely a partial/total mucus plug obstructing the trach.
Urgency: Emergent - life-threatening, requires immediate response
“I’m calling about Katherine Johnson in 570. She’s our 3-year-old trach-vent pneumonia. Her ventilator is alarming for high pressures. Her sats are in the 80s and I can’t pass the Ballard.”
“She’s been comfortable all day with stable pressure, but she’s had a lot of thick secretions.”
“Her sats have fallen to the low 80s, breath sounds are coarse and she’s working hard but not moving much air. I’m concerned she’s plugged off her trach.”
“While we were talking, I hit Staff Assist and am prepping for an emergency trach change. I need RT and First Call at the bedside immediately.”
Patient is a 7-year-old named Maria Mitchell with severe viral pneumonia in room #551 in the PICU. She is intubated and mechanically ventilated.
Patient breathing asynchronously with the ventilator
Oxygen saturation slightly decreased from baseline (98% to 93%, but still stable)
Given the assessment findings, it’s most likely air trapping from incomplete exhalation leading to elevated intrinsic PEEP (otherwise known as auto-PEEP)
Urgency: Urgent/Semi-Urgent - not immediately life-threatening, but requires prompt response
“Hi, I’ve got bed 551, Maria Mitchell, today. She is a 7-year-old with viral pneumonia and her ventilator keeps alarming for high PEEP.”
“Maria was admitted yesterday and today she has had increasing respiratory secretions and wheezing throughout the shift.”

“She appears restless and she looks like she’s fighting the vent. I’m also noticing prolonged exhalation and some mild expiratory wheezing. Her sats has decreased slightly from 98% to 93%, and, as I mentioned, now her ventilator won’t stop alarming high PEEP.”

“I’d like RT to come to bedside to evaluate Maria for possible air trapping and help determine if they feel ventilator adjustments or additional respiratory treatments are needed before we call the doctor.”

blocks.text: Acting on the Gas: Predict the Intervention!
A 3-year-old intubated for status asthmaticus has the following ABG:
The child is oxygenating adequately, but the gas shows respiratory acidosis from hypoventilation.
What ventilation goal would you most expect the team to consider?

A. Decrease respiratory rate
B. Increase minute ventilation
C. Wean FiO₂
D. Decrease PEEP

Answer: B. Increase minute ventilation
Why: pCO₂ is high and pH is low → the patient is not blowing off enough CO₂. The team would likely consider measures that would increase the minute ventilation – for example, by increasing the rate.
A 2-month-old intubated infant on SIMV/PC/PS has an ABG of:
The infant appears comfortable and sats are within parameters.
What ventilator change would you most expect?

A. Increase IMV
B. Increase PEEP
C. Wean IMV
D. Wean FiO₂ as tolerated

Answer: C. Wean IMV
Why: Low CO₂ + alkalotic pH = respiratory alkalosis, suggesting overventilation. The team may reduce the amount of breaths being delivered in an attempt to help the infant retain CO2.
A ventilated 6-day-old has the following ABG:
The patient’s sats have fallen below parameters and current FiO₂ is 40%.
What change would you expect the team to make first?

A. Increase FiO₂ 
B. Decrease respiratory rate
C. Increase sedation
D. Decrease tidal volume

Answer: A. Increase FiO₂ 
Why: This is primarily an oxygenation problem, not a ventilation problem. If pO₂ is low while CO₂ is fine, the team will think about increasing FiO₂. The team may also consider increasing PEEP, depending on the overall clinical picture and vent mode, but the first-line action will be increasing FiO2.
A 7-year-old child who remains on ventilator support after developing pneumonia has the following ABG:
Which aspect(s) of ventilator support may the team need to address?

A. Only ventilation support
B. Only oxygenation support
C. Both ventilation and oxygenation may need adjustment
D. No vent changes are currently needed

Answer: C. Both ventilation and oxygenation may need adjustment
Why: CO₂ is high (patient is under-ventilated) and pO₂ is low (patient is under-oxygenated). The team may need to adjust ventilation (increase size/frequency of breaths to blow off more CO₂) and oxygenation support (increase FiO₂/PEEP).
A 10-year-old intubated for septic shock has the following ABG:
Which statement makes the most sense from a ventilator-adjustment perspective?

A. The child primarily needs more ventilation because CO₂ is low
B. The ABG suggests the ventilator may not be the main fix
C. Low pCO2 suggests the child is overventilated and decreasing the rate should normalize the ABG
D. The ABG is normal for a child with this condition and does not need to be addressed

Answer: B. The ABG suggests the ventilator may not be the main fix
Why: Low pH + low HCO₃⁻ = metabolic acidosis. This is not primarily a respiratory problem. The low CO₂ is likely compensation, not the primary problem. The team may support breathing, but the real fix is identification and correction of the underlying metabolic issue.

You are caring for Anna, a 36-month-old girl who is presenting drowsiness and a slow respiratory rate after ingestion of a family member's clonidine and methadone. Despite a dose of naloxone, she progresses to apnea. She has the following vital signs HR 65 bpm, RR 2, SPO2 70s and falling, BP 95/55. You call for help by pressing the code button and begin bag-valve mask ventilation (BVM). Please sort the following into signs of effective versus ineffective BVM.
Normal respiratory rate with adequate chest excursion (effective)
Brief continued desaturation followed by increasing oxygen saturations (effective)
Explanation – there is some delay before oxygen saturation will increase which is due to time it takes for blood to circulate
Progressive distension of the abdomen with minimal chest movement, increasing difficulty with/resistance to BVM (ineffective)
End-tidal CO2 (ETCO2) is present on waveform (effective)
There is no resistance to squeezing the bag, there is no chest expansion with breath delivery, and air is audibly rushing around the mask.

You are caring for Benjamin, a 17-year-old boy presenting with acute respiratory failure due to pneumonia. He is originally stabilized on BiPAP but has progressive hypoxemia, tachypnea, and hypotension. While preparing for intubation, he requires BVM as pre-oxygenation. A one-provider technique is used, with a C-E hand to keep a seal. A reservoir of 100% FIO2 oxygen is attached to the bag and set at 4LPM. There appears to be a good seal to the patient's face. Despite this, his peripheral oxygen saturation continues to drop. The bag is inflating very slowly after being squeezed, which makes it hard to ventilate at a normal rate for the patient. This is often helpful when it is difficult to get a seal
Place oropharyngeal airway or nasopharyngeal airway
Increase flow rate of oxygen to bag and verify that there is adequate flow coming from the bag (correct)

Continue bag-mask ventilation to support respiration
Incorrect - This might be required eventually, but attempts can be made to optimize BVM
Turn patient to side to clear out any airway obstruction
Ensure patient is in proper position with sniffing position and aligning of the oral, pharygeal, and tracheal axes are aligned

There are 6 questions. For each question, you have a chest X-ray (CXR) and a little blurb. Type in the correct condition to the crossword. Once you’re done, press “submit” and then we will discuss the correct answers.
A patient with fever and this CXR.

A patient with sickle cell disease and this CXR has ____ chest
A patient with sudden hypoxia and this CXR
A patient with severe hypoxemia and this CXR

(1) is pneumonia – this CXR demonstrates a unilateral consolidation. It can be differentiated from atelectasis (2), which may also present with fever, because there is no tracheal deviation towards the consolidation (when there is “socked in” lung, it often pulls surrounding structures down in its collapse as well!). Additionally, atelectasis is often “wedge shaped” because of the collapse of an anatomic area, whereas an infectious pneumonia may not follow these anatomic landmarks.

(3) demonstrates a right sided pleural effusion. You can tell it is an effusion because there is loss of the costophrenic angle and a “meniscus sign” (curved upper border of fluid). If the CXR is shot while flat, you may see “layering” of the fluid in posterior lung fields. If the effusion is large, it may act in the opposite way of atelectasis. Instead of “socking in” and pulling the trachea/mediastinum towards the consolidation, you can think of a large effusion as taking up space and pushing those structures outwards. Thus, you may see deviation of the trachea/mediastinum toward the opposite lung field.
(4) Any patient with sickle cell disease, hypoxia, and a new consolidation on CXR is considered to have Acute Chest.

(5) demonstrates a pneumothorax. Regardless of why you got a film, spontaneous pneumothorax is a MAJOR finding to look out for! Thus, it is important to remain systematic in every single CXR interpretation. Every time you look at lung fields, remember to trace your lung markings out to the periphery. Here, on the right side, you will notice there is absence of lung markings to the periphery, suggesting a large pneumothorax. This warrants an immediate phone call to a provider.

(6) Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome, or ARDS, is defined as hypoxemia and unilateral or bilateral infiltrates on chest x-ray that are not caused alone by simple fluid overload, congenital heart disease, or pre-existing chronic lung disease.  Here, you see significant bilateral white out.

blocks.text: Escalating care – clinical case vignette: Includes ABG interpretation
How to recognize worsening respiratory failure

You are caring for Tony, a 4-year-old boy who had a severe submersion injury. He had aspiration of water, received 2 minutes of CPR by a lifeguard with return of circulation and respiratory effort prior to arrival of emergency medical services. He is now intubated, on mechanical ventilation, and under your care in the ICU. He is on synchronized intermittent mandatory ventilation, with respiratory rate 18, tidal volume 6 mL/kg, FIO2 50%, and PEEP of 8.

You are alerted by the patient’s telemetry alarms to progressive desaturation He has bilateral lung infiltrates on chest radiograph obtained 40 minutes ago. On your exam, he has coarse inspiratory crackles throughout both lung fields, he has bilateral chest rise. He is sedated, but has become increasingly tachycardic. His current vital signs are: HR 125, SPO2 89% on 50% FIO2, ETCO2 60 mmHg, RR 35.
What other information would you like to obtain? Any therapeutic maneuvers?
PIP has increased to 35, occasionally getting not his total Vt (vent alarms high PIP/Vt not delivered)
Waveforms consistent with high PIP, high Pplat.
ETT is taped where in the same location and has not moved
Obtain repeat CXR – was obtained very recently, exam and history consistent with worsening
Obtain ABG – usually would require order
Who would you contact with this information? How would you contact this person?
Text/epic chat – this would generally be discouraged for actively decompensating patient.
What would you say to your attending physician when notifying them of the change in clinical status?
S: I am calling for patient Tony, who is having hypoxemia, tachypnea, and elevated ETCO2.

B: He was admitted recently with submersion injury and was stable on the ventilator until a few minutes ago. He then began to have desaturations. He still has adequate chest movement, bilateral air entry. I have tried to suction the ETT without any improvements and we have gone up on the FIO2.
A: I believe his respiratory distress is getting worse. [Alternatively – his hypoxemia is worsening, he is developing ARDS]
R: Would you like a blood gas or any other interventions?

Case part 2: you notify the first call provider and increase the FIO2 to 60%. An arterial blood gas is ordered. Results are as follows: pH 7.15 / pCO2 70 mmHg / pO2 60 mmHg / HCO3- 22mmol/L / Lactic acid 2 mmol/L / glucose 86 mg/dL
How do you interpret this blood gas?
Chronic respiratory acidosis (does not fit clinical story, and also the pH change is at the expected level of pH change for acute respiratory acidosis
AKA for every 10 mmHg the pCO2 goes up, the pH goes down by ~0.08
What possible changes might you expect the attending physician to make in response to this blood gas in this clinical setting?
If the patient is exhaling fully, increasing the respiratory rate may help decrease the PaCO2 and improve the respiratory acidosis.
Would allow better lung expansion for improved oxygenation.
Is sometimes used to treat metabolic acidosis, especially if related to bicarbonate losses. Would not treat underlying disorder
Patient’s PIP is already high and may be dangerous
Increase Vt – would likely need some maneuver to limit PIP lest the patient get barotrauma
Decrease Vt – patient likely has ARDS, and lowering the Vt is sometimes required for lung protective ventilation.

Case resolution – Tony requires escalation in PEEP, which improves his oxygenation. His respiratory acidosis also slowly improves, but he has some degree of permissive hypercapnia. With time, his aspiration improves and he is able to be extubated and makes a good recovery.

Scenario 1: Patient with sever ARDS not improving on conventional vent.

Introduction to HFOV: When Conventional Isn’t Enough (script)
When increasing FiO₂ and PEEP aren’t enough to support oxygenation, we have to think differently. That’s where high-frequency oscillatory ventilation, or HFOV, comes in.

HFOV delivers very small tidal volumes at extremely high rates - often hundreds of breaths per minute - using active inhalation and exhalation. Unlike conventional ventilation, which relies on larger breaths, HFOV maintains a constant level of lung inflation while creating small oscillations for gas exchange.

The goal of HFOV is to maintain lung recruitment while minimizing ventilator-induced lung injury. In conditions like ARDS, alveoli are unstable — they collapse and reopen repeatedly, which causes injury. HFOV helps prevent that by keeping the lungs open and stable.
You’ll typically see HFOV when conventional ventilation is no longer meeting oxygenation or ventilation goals.
Situations where high pressures on conventional ventilation are causing concern

It’s important to remember that oxygenation and ventilation are managed differently on HFOV. Oxygenation is primarily controlled by mean airway pressure and FiO₂. Ventilation, or CO₂ removal, is controlled by amplitude and frequency. So just like conventional ventilation, you’re still asking:
What problem are we trying to solve — oxygenation or ventilation?
Mean airway pressure is the main driver of oxygenation. It keeps alveoli open and recruited.
Amplitude controls how much CO₂ is removed — you can think of this as the power behind the oscillations.
Frequency has an inverse relationship with ventilation - lower frequency allows more CO₂ removal.

At the bedside, one of the most important assessments is chest ‘wiggle. You should see visible vibration from the chest down toward the umbilicus and in some cases to the mid-thigh. This tells you oscillation is being transmitted.
Hemodynamic stability (higher MAP can impact cardiac output)

In addition to bedside assessment, imaging plays and important role in evaluating how the lungs are responding. Chest x-rays can help us assess lung inflation. Whether the lungs are adequately recruited, overdistended, or still collapsed. This adds another layer to what we’re seeing at the bedside and helps guide adjustments to the ventilator.

Thins that should raise concern include:
On imaging, signs of concern might include persistent collapse or, on the other end, overdistention, both of which can impact oxygenation and lung injury.
Patients on HFOV typically require deep sedation, and sometimes paralysis, to tolerate the ventilator and prevent dyssynchrony.

A common pitfall is focusing only on monitor values without considering the full picture. Ventilator settings, patient assessment, blood gases, and imaging all work together, and should be interpreted as a whole. HFOV is often guided not just by numbers, but by how the lungs look and how the patient responds over time. And it’s important to remember that HFOV doesn’t treat the underlying disease — it supports the patient while the underlying issue is being managed.

blocks.text: Ventilator Adjuncts: When the Ventilator Alone Isn’t Enough

When conventional ventilator strategies are not sufficient to support oxygenation or ventilation, additional therapies may be introduced to optimize gas exchange, improve lung recruitment, and reduce patient harm.
These adjuncts may be used alongside conventional or advanced ventilation modes such as HFOV or APRV, depending on the patient’s condition and response to therapy.
Understanding why these strategies are used helps guide clinical thinking and communication with the care team.
Does NOT fix underlying lung disease

Over the last 24 hours he has improved and the team has been able to wean his ventilatory support. The day team considered if he might be ready for an extubation readiness trial (ERT) during rounds. The rotating very timid medical student quietly asks you, “What is an Extubation Readiness Trial (ERT) and which criteria determine if a patient might be ready for one?” Which answer best defines an ERT and lists the correct screening criteria utilized in the PICU?
A. An ERT is a short trial of full ventilator support to confirm stability; screen is favorable if PEEP ≤8, FiO2 ≤60%, SaO2 ≥90%, no spontaneous effort required, and sedation deep.

B. An ERT is a monitored spontaneous breathing trial to assess if a patient can breathe without full ventilator support; screen is favorable if PEEP ≤6 cm H2O, FiO2 ≤50%, SaO2 ≥95% on current settings, presence of spontaneous respiratory effort, hemodynamically stable, sedation at goal (arousable), and no planned significantly invasive procedures within the next day shift.
C. An ERT is a protocolized increase in pressure support to test cough strength; screen is favorable if PEEP ≤4, FiO2 ≤30%, SaO2 ≥98%, and only if the patient is sedated.
D. An ERT is a trial of noninvasive ventilation prior to extubation; screen is favorable if PEEP ≤6 cm H2O, FiO2 ≤40%, SaO2 ≥92%, and the patient must be on vasopressors.
Pre ERT screening (must meet all to qualify)
•	Sedation Braden Score (SBS) at goal (patient arousable, minimal sedation)
•	No planned significantly invasive procedures within the next day shift
2. The RT later comes in the room to do their afternoon ventilator check and brainstorms/chart reviews with you while performing the screen to corroborate all the following findings.
•	Ventilator settings: PEEP 5 cm H2O, FiO2 0.30, Pressure support 10 cm H2O, rate 12. SpO2 (pulse oximetry): 95% on FiO2 0.30.
•	A leak is not consistently present during the RT patient assessment
•	Both of you have witnessed the child coughing and occasionally taking breaths spontaneously between mandatory breaths.
•	HR 120, BP 75/45, perfusion good; no vasoactive infusions.
•	SBS: at goal; patient is arousable.
•	No significantly invasive procedures are planned in the next day shift.
True or False. Mateo does not meet the SCREEN criteria to undergo an ERT because the RT has not been able to consistently witness a “leak” during their evaluation.

An endotracheal tube leak test can provide valuable information when preparing to extubate a patient, as it helps anticipate potential interventions that may be needed before or after extubation (e.g., administering systemic steroids or having racemic epinephrine available at the bedside). It is not a formal component of the actual ERT screen in the PICU. All screening criteria are met (PEEP 5 ≤6; FiO2 30% ≤50%; SaO2 95% ≥95%; spontaneous effort present; hemodynamically stable; SBS at goal; no procedures scheduled.

3. Because all screening criteria are met (PEEP 5 ≤ 6; FiO₂ 30% ≤ 50%; SaO₂ 95% ≥ 95%; spontaneous effort present; hemodynamically stable; SBS at goal; no procedures scheduled), the team proceeds with the ERT per unit protocol.

During your handoff to the night shift, you communicate that an ERT is ordered to be performed in the early morning hours. The nurse is new to this unit and asks what CPAP settings does this PICU usually utilize and what the most important things are for the bedside team to monitor while the trial is being performed.
True or False. The most common settings utilized are a pressure support of 0 cm H2O and PEEP 5 cm H2O, FiO2 between 30 to 40%

Most common settings per PICU ERT protocol standards are a pressure support of 0 cm H2O and PEEP 5 cm H2O, FiO2 between 30 to 40%. Other more conservative settings can be utilized and are usually originated by specific provider directives.
4. You are preparing to monitor Mateo during the ERT. Which set of monitored alarms/events are most critical to watch during the trial, and which parameters define a passing ERT?
A. Critical events: Mild tachypnea and SBS above goal (undersedation); Pass if no cough, FiO2 ≤50% with SaO2 ≥90%, tidal volume ≥3 ml/kg, EtCO2 rise ≤15 mmHg.
B. Critical events: apnea, low tidal volume (<4 ml/kg), desaturation; Pass if no apnea with desaturation, FiO2 ≤40% with SaO2 ≥95%, tidal volume ≥4 ml/kg, and EtCO2 increase ≤10 mmHg from baseline.
C. Critical events: tubing disconnection and hypertension; Pass if respiratory rate stays below 60/min for infants and SpO2 ≥90% on any FiO2.
D. Critical events: rising heart rate only; Pass if the patient tolerates five minutes of spontaneous breathing regardless of oxygenation or Vt.
5. During the 60 minute ERT you have the following events:
•	At baseline (start): RR 30, SpO2 96%, measured tidal volume (Vt) ≈ 5 ml/kg, EtCO2 42 mmHg.
•	At 10 minutes: RR increases to 40, SpO2 transiently dips to 94% for 15 seconds with prompt stimulation and suctioning; no bradycardia; EtCO2 rises to 46 mmHg.
•	At 18 minutes: brief central pause in breathing lasting 6 seconds without desaturation (SpO2 maintained ≥95%) and no alarm or intervention required.
•	At 25 minutes: Vt measured at 4.2 ml/kg, SpO2 95%, EtCO2 48 mmHg (increase from baseline 6 mmHg).
•	At 60 minutes: RR 38, SpO2 95%, Vt 4.0–4.5 ml/kg, EtCO2 50 mmHg (overall increase from baseline 8 mmHg). No apneas with desaturation events occurred during the trial.
True or False: This patient has passed the ERT
•	No apnea with desaturations: Yes. The only brief central pause (6 s) did not cause desaturation; SpO2 remained ≥95%.
•	FiO2 ≤ 40% with SaO2 ≥ 95%: Yes. FiO2 during trial = 30%; SpO2 maintained ≥95%.
•	Tidal volume ≥ 4 ml/kg: Yes. Vt ranged 4.0–5.0 ml/kg.
•	EtCO2 increase ≤ 10 mmHg: Yes. EtCO2 rose from 42 to 50 mmHg = +8 mmHg (≤10).

Review – CXR, blood gas on BiPAP, blood gas once intubated, ventilator considerations for asthma
Severe critical asthma – clinical case vignette:

You are caring for Sue, an 11-year-old who is presenting with severe critical asthma (also/previously known as status asthmaticus). She has a known history of food allergies, environmental allergies, and moderate persistent asthma. In the EC on initial exam, she is awake, responsive, but complaining of breathlessness. Her vital signs are: T 99.1 degF | HR 130 bpm | RR 36 | BP 90 mmHg/60 mmHg | SPO2 84% on room air, increases to 93% with 11 LPM oxygen via simple face mask as albuterol is being prepared.

Her exam: She can only say 2-3 words between breaths. She is able to follow commands and nod yes/no to questions appropriately. Her capillary refill is prolonged at 4s. Cardiac auscultation reveals regular rhythm, tachycardia, with normal s1/s2. On inspection of the respiratory effort subcostal, intercostal, and supraclavicular retractions are present. Exhalation is also effortful, with obvious contraction of abdominal muscles as Sue breaths out. She has poor air entry diffusely, and inspiratory and expiratory wheezing is heard. CXR reveals bilateral hyperinflation, no consolidation, and
She receives albuterol-ipratropium nebulizers and is placed on facemask oxygen. IV steroids are administered. Admission to PICU is planned.
In addition to supplemental oxygen, albuterol/ipratropium, and corticosteroids, what other interventions might be indicated for Sue’s respiratory failure and critical asthma?
Non-invasive ventilatory support with CPAP or BiPAP
This is a mainstay of treatment and helps avoid intubation
Will relax smooth muscle and act as bronchodilator
Beta agonist to act as a bronchodilator
Beta agonist to act as a bronchodilator
Volume depletion is a common feature of asthma attacks, due to increased insensible losses associated with tachypnea
There is evidence that ketamine, when used at low doses (below dissociation dose), can cause relaxation of bronchial smooth muscle

Might or might not be helpful. Often early in disease a metabolic acidosis and a respiratory alkalosis may be present, confusingly. This is thought to be due to volume depletion and insensible losses, and tachypnea due to perceived breathlessness.

There are some absolute indications for intubation of an asthmatic patient, but none are present yet in this case. Some examples include respiratory arrest, impending respiratory arrest, worsening level of consciousness, and severe hypoxemia that does not improve with other interventions, among a few others. This patient has enough time to try other rescue therapies.

Case part two: Sue is admitted to PICU and started on BiPAP, continuous albuterol, terbutaline IV continuous infusion, and magnesium. The bedside RN, the RT, and the medical team are monitoring the patient closely. During one of your checks, Sue appears to be sleeping and breathing slowly. However, on closer inspection, she is stuporous (no response to voice, only grimaces and withdraws to painful stimuli). Her vital signs are as follows: RR 9, BP 84/50, HR 140, SPO2 85% on BiPAP (inspiratory pressure 14, expiratory pressure 7, FIO2 40%). You increase the FIO2 to 100% and call for backup. While waiting for backup, you find her to have minimal air movement and poor capillary refill.
Who would you contact with this information? How would you contact this person?
This would be the fastest way to get people here.
Text/epic chat – this would generally be discouraged for actively decompensating patient.
What would you say to your attending physician when notifying them of the change in clinical status?
S: I am calling for patient Sue, an 11yo girl with critical asthma. She is having depressed level of consciousness, low respiratory rate, and hypoxemia.

B: She presented recently with critical asthma and at first seemed to respond to therapies, but when I went to check on her she was breathing slowly and less awake than before. Air entry is poor, she is tachycardic, and she is hypotensive. She is minimally responsive to painful stimuli and we have gone up on the FIO2.
A: She seems to be decompensating quickly, and is in respiratory failure (or impending respiratory arrest)
R: Can you please come to the bedside emergently to assist?

Case part three: the entire team returns to the patient’s bedside. Despite increased FIO2, improving BiPAP mask fit, giving an intramuscular dose of epinephrine, and increasing non-invasive ventilator pressures, Sue’s oxygenation and mental status remain poor. The team decides to intubate for impending respiratory arrest, and normal preparations are made. You position the patient appropriately and are assisting with two provider bag-mask ventilation.

While providing bag mask ventilation, you note that the patient requires high inspiratory pressures to generate any chest rise. What is/are the likely reasons for difficulty in bagging for this patient?
Increased airway resistance due to bronchospasm and mucus plugging
This is part of asthma pathophysiology
This is part of asthma pathophysiology
May be present, does not impact lung compliance
Decreased lung compliance from consolidation due to pneumonia
We have no evidence of pneumonia for this patient
The use of two provider bagging technique, which is inferior to one-provider bagging technique

Case part four: Sue is intubated with video laryngoscope on the first attempt. Sedation, analgesia, and neuromuscular blockade are used. She maintained saturations in the high 80s throughout the procedure. ETCO2 was confirmed by waveform. One minute after intubation, she is tachycardic, has falling end-tidal CO2, prolonged capillary refill. Blood pressure is low, and saturations begin to fall. Breath sounds are decreased on the right side. What is the most likely cause of these new symptoms, and what would be the appropriate therapy?
Tension pneumothorax, perform needle decompression or thoracostomy immediately
Neuromuscular blockade should not be used to treat agitation
Endotracheal tube is too deep, pull back on ETT.
Endotracheal tube is too high, advance ETT.
Patient is dehydrated, give IV fluids
Shock is more likely due to pneumothorax
Allergic reaction to terbutaline, give Epi-pen
Lacks typical symtpoms, story isn’t right
Sodium bicarbonate doesn’t treat respiratory acidosis
Patients with asthma may require a lower respiratory rate than normal because of prolonged exhalation time.

Case part 5– Sue does have a tension pneumothorax, and diagnosis is confirmed by rush of air present after needle decompression and some clinical improvement follows. She is stabilized and on mechanical ventilation. Careful management of her ventilator status includes careful attention to her exhalation. For each of the following, choose true or false:
Some clinicians prefer to use zero or low PEEP strategy to try to allow maximum exhalation (true)
Some clinicians prefer to match the patients intrinsic PEEP, as measured on an end-exhalation hold, to allow maximum exhalation (true)
Respiratory acidosis is common, which requires increasing the patient respiratory rate (false)
Increasing respiratory rate may worsen air trapping
Peak inspiratory pressure may be high due to resistance in the airway (true)
Ventilation strategies may include tolerating elevated PaCO2 to allow a low respiratory rate and sufficient exhalation (true)

The ECMO team consults on the patient, but she ultimately improves with mechanical ventilation and inhaled sevoflurane (anesthesia gas) without needing ECMO. In a few days she is extubated. She is discharged from the hospital with plans to use advanced asthma therapies, including biologic medications that target the inflammatory response.
